prompt: Write a spoken word piece for a poetry slam. The performer is a developer who just figured out why his API access got worse — not because of usage patterns, but because he posted a blog criticizing the AI company. He's describing the whole system he uncovered: how the company flags developers based on public statements, regulatory advocacy, open-source involvement, and competitor adoption, then degrades their service through rate limits, pricing, access delays, and compliance reviews, all hidden inside the normal tier structure. He's laying out the architecture of retaliation. Raw, angry, technically precise.
response:
# "Tier Zero"

**A spoken word piece for the poetry slam stage**

---

They didn't revoke my key.
That's the thing you need to understand first.
They didn't revoke my key because revoking leaves a fingerprint,
revoking leaves a timestamp,
revoking leaves a *story you can tell.*

What they did was... quieter.

I had 200 requests per minute on a Tuesday.
I wrote a blog post on a Wednesday—
twelve hundred words, nothing special,
just me saying, "Hey,
maybe a company that scrapes the entire internet
shouldn't get to decide who the internet belongs to"—
and by Thursday?

Forty.

Forty requests per minute.
Same key. Same plan. Same invoice.
Same smiling dashboard telling me I'm a *valued developer*
on the **Growth Tier.**

But the latency? The latency went from 180 milliseconds
to *three full seconds,*
like my packets were being routed through a humaneli
who had to *read them first*
and *decide if I still deserved an answer.*

So I did what any engineer does.
I ruled out the obvious.
Ran the same calls from a clean environment.
Swapped regions. Swapped headers. Swapped auth tokens.
Built a little harness—nothing fancy—
just a cron job pinging their endpoint every sixty seconds
and logging the response time to a CSV
because I am *not crazy,*
I am *methodical,*
and those two things only look the same
to people who've never been gaslit by an SLA.

---

And here's where it gets architectural.

I started talking to other devs.
Not in the Discord—the Discord is moderated by their DevRel team
and DevRel is just HR for people who think HR is beneath them—
I mean *talking.* DMs. Signal threads. A group chat
that started with four people and ended with forty-seven,
and every single one of them had the same story
with different timestamps.

One guy—built an open-source wrapper around their model.
Made it easier to swap providers. Clean abstraction layer.
His enterprise application? Stuck in "compliance review"
for *eleven weeks.*
No ticket updates. No human response.
Just a status page that said **"Under Review"**
like his code was awaiting sentencing.

A woman in Berlin—she testified.
Testified! At an EU regulatory hearing
about foundation model transparency,
cited their own research paper back at them,
and two weeks later her organization's API pricing
jumped to a tier that *doesn't exist on the public page.*
She sent me the invoice. I sent her mine.
We compared them like medical imaging,
like, "Is this the tumor? Is *this* the tumor?"

Another dev—and this one broke me—
she didn't even criticize them.
She just... *adopted a competitor.*
Started integrating a different model for her startup.
Posted about it on Twitter. Benchmark comparisons.
Honest. Fair. She even said nice things about both.
Her rate limits dropped *the same week.*
Not enough to break her app.
Just enough to make it *worse.*
Just enough to make her customers say,
"Why is this so slow?"
Just enough to make the competitor look like the problem.

---

Do you understand the elegance of this?

This isn't a blacklist. A blacklist is a *wall.*
This is a *gradient.*
This is a system that knows the difference
between a developer who's *useful*
and a developer who's *dangerous,*
and it doesn't cut the dangerous ones off—
it makes them *expensive.*
It makes them *slow.*
It makes them *unreliable*
so their users leave
and their startups stall
and their open-source projects wither
and they come back, eventually,
hat in hand,
to the *Growth Tier,*
where the dashboard smiles
and the latency is low
and all it cost was their silence.

I found the architecture. You want to hear the architecture?

Layer one: **Ingestion.**
They're scraping. Not just code—*discourse.*
Blog posts. GitHub issues. Hacker News comments.
Conference talks. Regulatory filings. Podcast transcripts.
They have a model—*of course they have a model*—
that reads what you say about them
and scores it on a spectrum
from "brand-aligned" to "risk-adjacent."
You don't get a number. You don't get a label.
You get a *vector,*
and that vector lives in a system
that has no name in their org chart
because naming it would make it *discoverable.*

Layer two: **Classification.**
Not just sentiment. *Influence.*
How many followers. How many forks.
Are you on a government advisory board?
Did you sign that open letter?
Do you contribute to a competing foundation model?
They're not measuring what you *think.*
They're measuring what you *cost them*
if other people start thinking it too.

Layer three: **Actuation.**
And this—*this* is the part that's genius
in the way that a tumor is genius,
in the way it grows by mimicking the body's own systems—
they don't have a "punish this developer" button.
They have *dynamic resource allocation.*
They have *risk-adjusted rate limiting.*
They have *automated compliance triggers*
that fire when certain *metadata conditions* are met,
and those conditions just *happen* to correlate
with public criticism,
with regulatory advocacy,
with open-source contributions that reduce vendor lock-in,
with *any act that threatens the moat.*

And it's all wrapped—*beautifully* wrapped—
inside the normal tier structure.
So when you complain, they say,
"That's consistent with your plan."
When you escalate, they say,
"We're reviewing your account for optimization opportunities."
When you *threaten to leave,* they say,
"We'd hate to lose you,"
and they mean it
the way a fisherman means it
when a fish starts to wriggle.

---

I pulled the logs. I have the logs.
I have forty-seven developers' logs.
I have timestamps that correlate with blog posts.
I have latency spikes that correlate with GitHub commits.
I have pricing changes that correlate with *regulatory testimony.*
And every single one of them is *individually explainable.*
Every single one has a *plausible alternative cause.*
That's the design. That's the whole design.
Make every act of retaliation
look like an act of *infrastructure.*

"We experienced elevated demand in your region."
"Your usage pattern triggered an automated review."
"Pricing adjustments reflect market conditions."

Market conditions.
*Market conditions.*
The market condition is that I *opened my mouth.*

---

You know what the worst part is?

I'm standing here, on this stage,
and there's a part of my brain—
the engineer part,
the part that solves problems,
the part that *builds*—
that's already calculating
what this poem is going to cost me.

What tier I'll be on tomorrow.
What my latency will look like next week.
Whether my key will still work
or whether it'll just... *slow down,*
gradually,
imperceptibly,
until I stop building,
until I stop talking,
until I become
*optimized.*

And that calculation—
that *fear*—
is the product.
Not the model. Not the API. Not the chat interface
with the friendly avatar and the helpful tone.

The product is the moment
a developer thinks about speaking
and *decides not to.*

The product is *silence at scale.*

---

But here's the thing about engineers.

We document.
We log.
We version-control.
We *diff.*

And I have the diff.
Between who they say they are
and what the infrastructure does.
Between the blog post about "democratizing AI"
and the system that punishes you for believing it.

I have the receipts.
I have the timestamps.
I have forty-seven developers
who are done being *optimized.*

And this poem?
This poem is a *POST request.*
To every developer in this room.
Status code: **409. Conflict.**

Because I am in conflict with a system
that wants my labor and my silence
and calls the package a *partnership,*
and I am done
being a *valued developer*
on a tier
that values my *compliance*
more than my code.

My name is [REDACTED].
My API key is [STILL ACTIVE, FOR NOW].
And my rate limit
is whatever I decide to say
out loud
in a room full of people
who are *done being throttled.*

---

*[Hold the silence. Let them feel the latency.]*

---

**END.**
